Texas Oil & Gas Workers End Six-Day Strike, Operations Resume Across Permian Basin

MIDLAND, Texas — Hundreds of oil and gas workers returned to drilling sites and production facilities across the Permian Basin on Tuesday morning, following a six-day strike that temporarily slowed crude output in one of America’s most vital energy regions. The walkout, which began last Wednesday, saw employees from several contractors and operators—including Red Mesa Energy, Lone Star Drilling, and Tri-County Resources—down tools in protest over pay and workplace safety concerns.

The United Oil & Gas Workers Union (UOGWU) confirmed late Monday that a tentative agreement had been reached with representatives from the Permian Producers Association, ending the strike and clearing the way for production to restart at dozens of affected rigs and processing plants.

“We’re pleased to announce our members will be returning to work under improved terms,” said UOGWU regional vice president Martha Chavez. “Our members stood together for fair wages and better safety protocols, and we believe this agreement delivers on both fronts.”

The strike, the largest in the Permian since 2016, saw an estimated 1,400 workers participate, temporarily halting drilling and maintenance operations at key sites. Analysts at West Texas Energy Insights estimate crude production in the affected fields fell by up to 160,000 barrels per day during the stoppage, though most companies maintained minimum staffing to ensure safety and equipment integrity.

Red Mesa Energy spokesperson Daniel Price acknowledged the disruption, saying, “We respect our workers’ right to be heard, and we’re relieved to have reached common ground. Our immediate focus is bringing operations back online safely and efficiently.”

Details of the settlement include a phased 7% wage increase over the next 18 months and a joint labor-management task force to address workplace safety improvements. According to union officials, the task force will begin meeting within 30 days to review and recommend enhancements to site protocols and equipment standards.

Local officials, already concerned about the economic impact of the work stoppage, welcomed the resolution. “Our community relies on these jobs and this industry,” said Midland County Judge Carlos Mendoza. “It’s a relief to see everyone coming back to work and production getting back up to speed.”

Industry groups expect oil output to return to pre-strike levels within the week, with minimal long-term impacts. Union leaders described the agreement as a “turning point” for labor relations in the region’s oilfields.
